\section{How Brokers Accumulate Informational and Structural Advantage: A Formal Illustration}

\subsection{Model and Methods}

I use an agent-based model (ABM) to formalize the theory. The model is a formal illustration, not a test of the theory; it serves as a bridge from theory to testable propositions. Complete pseudocode and specifications appear in Appendices A and B. The public git repository (\texttt{https://github.com/m-laprise/brokerage-abm}) contains the Julia code and scripts needed to reproduce the simulations, statistics, figures, and manuscript text.

The model isolates the informational consequences of outsourced relational work. Principals learn only from their own matches, whereas the broker pools information from matches it mediates across principals. Learning general quality represents attributional assessment, while learning complementarity represents relational assessment. The broker represents the information-aggregating function of corporate brokerage, not its internal organization, and the model does not simulate the later transition to resource capture or data enclosure.

\emph{Market and match output}. Principals are the market participants seeking partners. Many principals and one broker occupy an undirected network. The model represents match quality as match output. Each principal has a fixed vector of observable characteristics, which defines its type. For any potential pair, expected match output is determined by the two principals' types and by fixed features of the matching environment drawn at the start of each simulation run. It combines general quality, which depends on each principal separately, and complementarity, which depends on how their types interact (Appendix B \S2).

Before they are combined, the two components are centered and scaled to have the same variance. The parameter $\rho$ sets their relative contributions to variation in expected match output: general quality contributes a fraction $\rho$, and complementarity contributes $1-\rho$. Thus, $\rho=0$ represents pure complementarity and $\rho=1$ represents pure general quality. The parameter $\delta$ controls how sharply complementarity changes across a boundary in type-pair space: it multiplies complementarity by $1+\delta$ on one side and $1-\delta$ on the other. Larger values make otherwise similar pairs on opposite sides of the boundary differ more in expected output, making complementarity harder to learn. A common normalization holds the average within-market variance of expected match output constant as $\rho$ and $\delta$ vary. Because $\delta$ affects only complementarity, it has no effect when $\rho=1$.

When a pair matches, its realized output equals its expected output plus an independent, mean-zero random shock. This shock represents match-specific variation that neither the principals nor the broker can anticipate. Supplementary Figures S1--S3 visualize the type distribution, expected match output, and its effective dimensionality.

\emph{Search, matching, and learning}. Each period, principals seek pairwise matches either through self-search or through the broker (Appendix A \S\S5--7; Appendix B \S\S6--7). They choose one channel using satisfaction with past realized output net of search costs or broker fees. Self-search considers existing neighbors and a random sample of other principals. The broker considers principals in its standing roster, its persistent list of contacts, and those currently using its services. Principals estimate expected output from their own match histories. The broker pools the matches it has mediated and uses both parties' characteristics, without privileging either party. Each uses a small neural network for these predictions.

Estimated output determines how candidates are ranked. For previously matched neighbors, self-search instead uses the pair's average past realized output. Tied estimates are ordered uniformly at random. Principals make offers to the highest-ranked candidates whose estimated output exceeds the reservation threshold, the minimum required for an offer. All offers enter a common market. A completed match produces realized output and creates a direct tie that persists until either principal exits. Each principal observes the partner's type and realized output from its own matches; the broker observes both types and realized output from every match it mediates. At the end of each period, every principal exits independently with probability $\eta$ and is replaced by a new entrant.

\emph{Measurement}. The outsourcing rate is the share of requested match positions routed through the broker. A brokered placement is classified as access when it creates a direct tie between previously unconnected principals and as assessment when it reuses an existing tie. The access fraction is the share of brokered placements classified as access. It measures network-expanding brokerage, not whether a counterparty was impossible to discover through self-search. The output gap is the difference in mean realized output between brokered matches and self-search matches. Broker betweenness centrality measures the share of shortest paths between principals that pass through the broker (Brandes 2001; Freeman 1977). Supplementary Figures S4--S6 reproduce the structural analyses using Burt's constraint and effective size.

Prediction quality is evaluated each period using randomly sampled potential partners. These evaluations do not update either model, although a sampled pair may have matched previously. Predictions are compared with expected output, without a random shock. Rank correlation is Spearman's correlation between the candidate ordering produced by predicted output and the ordering produced by expected output; tied predictions are ordered uniformly at random before the correlation is calculated. The ranking advantage is the broker's rank correlation minus the principals' rank correlation. $R^2$ measures accuracy in predicting expected output levels, but is diagnostic only. It can become extremely negative when expected output varies little across the sampled candidates and is not used in any choice made by the principals or broker (Appendix B \S8).

\emph{Simulation design and analysis}. At the baseline, $N=1{,}000$ principals interact for $T=500$ periods with $\rho=0.5$, $\delta=0.5$, and $\eta=0.02$. One-at-a-time (OAT) sweeps vary the matching problem, turnover, market size, reservation threshold, initial network, broker roster, and self-search pool. Four two-parameter grids cross $\rho$ with $\eta$, $\rho$ with the reservation threshold, $\eta$ with the reservation threshold, and $\rho$ with $\delta$ (Appendix B \S9). I refer to each unique model configuration as a regime. Together, the sweeps and grids contain \pv{nRegimes} regimes. There are \pv{nGeneralSeeds} random seeds per regime and \pv{nBaselineSeeds} at the baseline (\pv{nRuns} runs total).

Neural-network performance depends on the learning rate and the number of training updates, so I calibrated these settings before running the main simulations. I compared candidate settings for principals and the broker separately, considering ranking performance on randomly sampled candidates, stability over time and across random seeds, and computational time. I then confirmed the selected settings together using five additional calibration seeds that were not used in the reported simulations. The candidate settings and seed-level results are preserved in the replication code.

To assess whether the findings depend on neural-network learning, I repeat the complete design with Ridge regression. In the unrestricted Ridge specification, principals use candidate characteristics, while the broker uses both parties' characteristics and interactions between them. Ridge penalties were calibrated at the baseline using ranking performance on randomly sampled candidates and random seeds excluded from the reported simulations. Three additional Ridge experiments, conducted at the baseline and across the $\rho\times\delta$ grid, restrict the broker by giving it the same number of observations as a typical principal, retaining only one party's characteristics from each match, or omitting interactions between the two parties' characteristics. The complete calibration and experimental procedures are preserved in the replication code.

Ensemble means are averages across random seeds. Late-window means first average periods $t\in[481,500]$ within each random seed and then average those seed-level values; early-window means use $t\in[50,70]$. Cross-regime summaries give each regime equal weight. Intervals for differences are calculated within each random seed before being combined across seeds. Time-series figures begin at $t=30$ to omit the initialization transient, without changing the simulations or reported averages. Monte Carlo convergence was assessed in two ways. For each regime and reported outcome, I calculated a two-sided 95\% confidence interval for the mean across independent random seeds using the $t$ distribution. I also compared nested estimates based on the first 10 versus all 20 seeds outside the baseline and the first 20 versus all 50 seeds at the baseline. Across the \pv{mcOutcomeCount} non-$R^2$ figure outcomes, the median across regimes of the confidence-interval half-width divided by the absolute estimate based on all available seeds ranged from \pv{mcCiMedianMinPercent}\% to \pv{mcCiMedianMaxPercent}\%. The median across regimes of the absolute difference between the nested estimates, divided by the same full estimate, ranged from \pv{mcNestedMedianMinPercent}\% to \pv{mcNestedMedianMaxPercent}\%. These relative quantities are not reported when the full-sample interval includes zero because division by an estimate near zero is unstable; those cases are assessed in the outcome's original units.

\subsection{The Broker Primarily Provides Assessment, Not Access}

Across the tested regimes, the broker is usually the dominant channel in the market. The outsourcing rate as a share of demand is \pv{outBaselineLate} at the baseline (late mean, up from an early mean of \pv{outBaselineEarly}) and has a median of \pv{outBaseMed} across regimes. It exceeds one-half in \pv{outBaseDominantN} of \pv{nRegimes} regimes; the remaining regimes all have no turnover. Yet the broker primarily assesses options within the existing network rather than providing access beyond it. The access fraction (the share of brokered placements between principals with no pre-existing tie) has a late mean of \pv{accessAcrossBaseLate} across regimes, down from \pv{accessAcrossBaseEarly} early, and never exceeds \pv{accessBaseMax}. \ifnum\pv{accessDeclineCIN}=\pv{nRegimes}\relax It declines over time in all regimes, and its paired 95\% interval is below zero in every regime.\else It declines significantly in \pv{accessDeclineCIN} of \pv{nRegimes} regimes.\fi\ Most brokered matches therefore connect principals already tied to each other. Figure~\ref{fig:dynamics} and Table~\ref{tab:baseline-measures} summarize these baseline dynamics and the main measures.

At the baseline, the broker's realized-output advantage develops as the market evolves: the output gap (broker minus self-search) changes from $\pv{ogapBaselineEarly}$ early to $\pv{ogapBaselineLate}$ late. Across regimes, mean realized output is higher through the broker channel in \pv{ogapBasePosN} of \pv{nRegimes} regimes, and the late output gap averages $\pv{ogapBaseMean}$. Paired 95\% Monte Carlo intervals are above zero in \pv{ogapBaseCIPosN} regimes and below zero in \pv{ogapBaseCINegN}. The negative gaps occur in \pv{ogapBaseNegN} regimes, all with no or nearly no turnover ($\eta\in\{0,0.001\}$). Principals choose a channel using satisfaction scores that include unfilled requests, fees, and search costs, whereas the output gap compares realized output among completed matches. Outsourcing is therefore not itself evidence that the broker always produces better matches.

The broker's assessment advantage appears more consistently in ranking candidates than in predicting expected output levels. Among randomly sampled potential partners (Appendix~A~\S8), its rank correlation is \pv{brokerRankBaseline} at the baseline and has a median of \pv{brokerRankBaseMed} across regimes, compared with \pv{agentRankBaseline} and \pv{agentRankBaseMed} for principals. The broker-minus-principal difference in rank correlation is positive in \pv{rankGapNNPosN} of \pv{nRegimes} regimes, with paired 95\% intervals above zero in \pv{rankGapNNCiPosN} regimes. Ranking determines which candidates are considered first, while predicted levels also determine whether offers clear the reservation threshold. Accurate ranking is therefore more important than accurate prediction of expected output levels, although both can affect matching.

Most brokered placements therefore reuse ties that principals could search directly; relatively few expand the principal network. The broker's ranking advantage appears under pure general quality as well as complementarity: at $\rho=1$, the broker-minus-principal difference in rank correlation averages \pv{rhoOneRankGapMean} and is positive in all \pv{rhoOneRankGapPosN} pure-quality regimes. The OAT checks also show that initial network degree ($k_G$), broker roster fraction, and the number of strangers available in self-search have comparatively small effects on the main economic outcomes.

\subsection{The Broker's Information Advantage Comes from Data Volume and Relational Information}

The theory identifies two sources of the broker's information advantage: the greater volume of observations generated by working across principals and relational information about both parties to each match. The Ridge experiments separate these sources from the flexibility of the neural network. When Ridge regression replaces both neural networks, the broker-minus-principal difference in rank correlation is \pv{ridgeBaselineGap} at the baseline, has a median of \pv{ridgeMedianGap} across the \pv{ridgeNConditions} regimes, and is positive in all \pv{ridgePositiveN}. The full Ridge model still gives the broker more observations and more information about each pair than a principal. Because each restriction changes later matching and learning, their effects need not be additive.

Data volume accounts for much of the advantage (Fig.~\ref{fig:information-sources}). Across the \pv{ablationConditionN} regimes in the baseline and $\rho\times\delta$ design, the median broker-minus-principal difference in rank correlation is \pv{ablationPairMedianGap} in the full Ridge model but only \pv{ablationSizeMedianGap} when the broker trains on the same number of observations as a typical principal. The difference remains positive in \pv{ablationSizePositiveN} of \pv{ablationConditionN} regimes under this restriction, so data volume is important without being the broker's only advantage.

The content of the broker's data also matters. When each observation retains the characteristics of only one party to a match, the broker's median advantage over principals in ranking new candidates is \pv{ablationSingleMedianGap} and remains positive in only \pv{ablationSinglePositiveN} of the \pv{ablationConditionN} tested regimes. Retaining both parties' characteristics improves on this one-party version in \pv{ablationAdditiveBeatsSingleN} of \pv{ablationConditionN} regimes, and retaining how those characteristics interact improves it further in \pv{ablationPairBeatsAdditiveN} of \pv{ablationConditionN} regimes. Interaction information matters most when complementarity contributes strongly to expected match output and not at all under pure general quality. The broker's advantage therefore comes from both the volume of observations generated through repeated vicarious relational work and information about how the characteristics of two parties combine.

\subsection{The Nature of the Matching Problem Shapes the Broker's Advantage}
\label{sec:matching-shapes}

The model separates two features of assessment: whether expected match output depends on general quality or pair-specific complementarity, and how difficult complementarity is to learn. The parameter $\rho$ moves expected match output from pure complementarity at $\rho=0$ toward pure general quality at $\rho=1$. The parameter $\delta$ increases difficulty by making expected output change more sharply across a boundary in type-pair space. Because complementarity disappears at $\rho=1$, $\delta$ has no effect there. The pure-quality case is therefore a separate boundary condition, not a smooth continuation of the interior $\rho$ values.

Broker centrality is governed primarily by the composition of expected match output. In the one-at-a-time sweep from $\rho=0$ to $\rho=0.85$, the access fraction rises from \pv{accessRho0} to \pv{accessRho085} and broker betweenness centrality falls from \pv{betwRho0} to \pv{betwRho085}. The $\rho\times\eta$ grid shows the same directions at every turnover rate. At the pure-quality boundary, centrality falls further to \pv{betwRho1}, while access returns to \pv{accessRho1}. The boundary therefore extends the decline in centrality but not the increase in access below $\rho=1$.

Under pure complementarity, greater difficulty lowers the ranking accuracy of both the broker and principals, but it does not eliminate the broker's advantage. Increasing $\delta$ from 0 to 1 lowers the broker's rank correlation from \pv{brokerRankRho0D0} to \pv{brokerRankRho0D1} and the principal correlation from \pv{agentRankRho0D0} to \pv{agentRankRho0D1} (Fig.~\ref{fig:grid}). The corresponding broker-minus-principal differences are \pv{rankGapRho0D0} and \pv{rankGapRho0D1}. The size of this difference is not monotonic in difficulty, but its paired 95\% interval is above zero in \pv{gridRankGapCIPosN} of the \pv{rhoDeltaEffectiveN} regimes. Because $\delta$ changes only complementarity, it is inactive at the pure-quality boundary.

The broker's realized-output advantage is greatest when expected match output depends more heavily on complementarity. Paired 95\% intervals for the broker-minus-self-search output gap are above zero in \pv{gridOutputGapCIPosN} of the \pv{rhoDeltaEffectiveN} regimes. Composition and difficulty therefore shape different outcomes. Greater difficulty makes candidates harder for both sides to rank but does not produce a monotonic change in the broker's relative ranking advantage. Greater reliance on complementarity increases the mean realized output produced through brokered matches. The broker retains both a ranking advantage and an output advantage throughout the grid.

\subsection{A Broker Can Be Highly Central While Doing Little Bridging}

In most regimes, the broker's structural position strengthens over time while principals have fewer direct ties on average. At the baseline, mean principal degree falls from \pv{degBaselineEarly} to \pv{degBaselineLate}, while broker betweenness centrality rises from \pv{betwBaselineEarly} to \pv{betwBaselineLate} (early to late means). This combination occurs in \pv{comoveN} of \pv{nRegimes} regimes, and principal degree falls in \pv{degFallsN} of them (Fig.~\ref{fig:position}). In most regimes, direct ties do not accumulate fast enough to offset turnover. The broker's structural advantage therefore does not disappear as brokered matches create direct ties. Because outsourcing connects current clients to the broker, sustained use converts the value of assessment into structural centrality.

The distinction between assessment and access helps explain this relationship. An access match creates a direct tie between previously unconnected principals and can remove the broker from their shortest path. An assessment match reuses an existing tie, so the broker can serve the market without directly adding ties to the principal network. The two controlled comparisons in Figure~\ref{fig:position} separate matching composition from turnover. Holding turnover fixed, moving from pure complementarity toward $\rho=0.85$ raises access and lowers centrality. Holding $\rho$ fixed, increasing turnover raises both access and centrality at every tested $\rho$. Turnover creates network gaps, while matching composition determines how often brokerage closes them with direct ties.

The turnover effect is substantial but nonlinear. Holding other parameters at baseline, increasing $\eta$ from 0 to 0.03 lowers late mean principal degree from \pv{degEta0Late} to \pv{degEta003Late} and raises broker centrality from \pv{betwEta0Late} to \pv{betwEta003Late}, with most of the change occurring between $\eta=0.001$ and $0.01$. Turnover also changes the broker's realized-output advantage. In the $\rho\times\eta$ grid, the 95\% interval for the broker-minus-self-search output gap is below zero in \pv{qgapEta0CINegN} of \pv{rhoEtaRhoN} $\rho$ conditions at $\eta=0$, but above zero in \pv{qgapEta01CIPosN} of \pv{rhoEtaRhoN} by $\eta=0.01$. In the model, turnover removes principals and ties, creating network gaps and the conditions under which brokered matches outperform self-search.

\begin{figure}
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/centrality_and_access.png}
\caption{\textbf{\pvtitle{position}.} \pvcaption{position}}
\label{fig:position}
\end{figure}

The pure-quality boundary confirms that low access alone is not sufficient for high centrality. Although higher turnover raises centrality there, centrality remains below pure complementarity at the same turnover rate. In the tested regimes, high centrality occurs when turnover renews network gaps and brokerage mainly assesses existing relationships.

\begin{figure}
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.92\linewidth]{figures/structural_advantage.png}
\caption{\textbf{\pvtitle{advantage}.} \pvcaption{advantage}}
\label{fig:advantage}
\end{figure}

Figure~\ref{fig:advantage} shows that structural position relates differently to relative ranking and realized match output. Holding all other parameters fixed, moving from pure complementarity to pure general quality reduces the output gap from \pv{ogapRho0Group} to \pv{ogapRho1Group}, while increasing the broker-minus-principal difference in rank correlation from \pv{rankGapRho0Group} to \pv{rankGapRho1Group}. The broker is therefore most central and produces its largest realized-output advantage where its advantage over principals in ranking candidates is smaller. Taken together, the results separate the sources of informational, economic, and structural advantage. Observing matches across clients, while retaining information about both parties, improves candidate ranking. Complementarity increases the realized output produced by brokered matches. Turnover repeatedly removes ties, renewing the network gaps that support broker centrality. These advantages need not move together.

\subsection{Propositions}

The simulation results motivate the following falsifiable propositions for future empirical research. These propositions extend the model's implications beyond the simulated setting:

\noindent\textbf{P1.} In markets where match quality depends on complementarity, brokers add value primarily by assessing reachable counterparties rather than by bridging disconnected parties. The value of this assessment role increases as complementarity contributes more to match quality.

\noindent\textbf{P2.} A broker's betweenness centrality is produced by sustained outsourcing, which depends on client satisfaction. It is greater where match quality depends more heavily on complementarity, and assessment-heavy brokers tend to retain or gain centrality as networks evolve.

\noindent\textbf{P3.} Holding market turnover constant, bridging position and bridging behavior are negatively related: assessment-heavy brokers tend to be more central while doing less bridging. Higher turnover can raise both access and centrality by continually creating new network gaps.

\noindent\textbf{P4.} Brokers can provide superior assessment by ranking potential matches better than principals even when their predictions of expected output levels are inaccurate.

These propositions explain how brokers accumulate and sustain informational and structural advantages. The next section considers how a corporate broker may convert accumulated information into resource capture or data enclosure.
